title: Tigney Technology Inc. (Feb 2000 FCA) SR&ED Decision
subject: FCA appeal on whether SR&ED work physically performed outside Canada could earn investment tax credits.
outcome: Crown's appeal allowed in part; FCA reversed the TCC on the Kentucky work, holding expenditures outside Canada earn no ITCs.
summary: Tigney Technology (2000 FCA) is a Federal Court of Appeal SR&ED decision holding that Canadian taxpayers cannot claim investment tax credits under the Income Tax Act on experimental work physically performed outside Canada, even when it is integral to a Canadian-directed project. The Tax Court also disallowed circular intercompany management fees as mere book entries, not expenditures made.
metaDescription: Examine the February 2000 Federal Court of Appeal ruling for Tigney Technology Inc. on Canadian SR&ED tax credit claims.

body.text: Executive Summary & Case Background

The decision of the Federal Court of Appeal in Her Majesty The Queen v. Tigney Technology Incorporated (2000 DTC 6112; 2000 CanLII 14892 (FCA); Docket A-70-97 and A-303-97), rendered on February 7, 2000, stands as a foundational precedent in Canadian Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax law. Heard in tandem with the companion appeal in LGL Limited v. Her Majesty The Queen (Docket A-139-99), the unanimous ruling delivered by Justice McDonald (with Justices Robertson and Rothstein concurring) reversed in part the earlier judgment of Judge Bell at the Tax Court of Canada (Tigney Technology Incorporated v. Her Majesty the Queen, 97 DTC 414; [1997] 2 C.T.C. 2333 (TCC); Docket 95-2794(IT)G, decided January 9, 1997). Together, the Tax Court of Canada and Federal Court of Appeal judgments establish two enduring principles governing claims for SR&ED deductions under section 37 and Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) under section 127 of the Canadian Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (then cited as R.S.C. 1952, c. 148) (the "Act"). First, an SR&ED project cannot be treated as an indivisible geographical whole for the purpose of qualifying foreign-executed activities for Canadian ITCs; even where experimental testing or data collection performed outside Canada is an indispensable, integral component of a broader SR&ED project conceived, directed, and analyzed in Canada, the constituent activities physically performed outside Canada are excluded from paragraph 37(1)(a) of the Act and cannot generate ITCs. Second, notional intercompany management fees recorded solely via circular accounting journal entries between a parent corporation and its wholly owned research subsidiary do not constitute "expenditures made" or "incurred" on SR&ED under section 37 of the Act and section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations (the "Regulations").
Factual Matrix and Taxpayer's Claim

Tigney Technology Incorporated ("TTI") was a Canadian corporation based in Edmonton, Alberta, engaged in the business of conducting scientific research and seeking to commercialize the resulting intellectual property. TTI's core technological focus involved a specialized biomass hydrolysis and fractionation process designed to separate the constituent components of lignocellulosic plant materials—such as trees, straw, and bagasse—into industrial sugars and non-cellulosic fractions while preserving the chemical integrity of the separated materials. To structure its operations, TTI incorporated a subsidiary corporation, Tigney Research Incorporated ("TRI" or "Research"), with the corporate mandate to perform and account for all research conducted on behalf of TTI.

The dispute before the Canadian courts encompassed TTI's 1993 and 1994 taxation years, with fiscal periods running from June 1 to May 31 of the following calendar year. Two distinct clusters of claimed SR&ED expenditures were at issue across these taxation years. The first cluster involved cross-border experimental expenditures incurred in connection with Swedish Tobacco during the 1993 taxation year. In late 1990, Dr. Curt Enzell, an official with Swedish Tobacco, contacted TTI after learning of its plant-fractionation research. Swedish Tobacco was attempting to produce a safer cigarette, which necessitated the extraction of specific chemical compounds from tobacco leaves. TTI initially performed laboratory experiments in Edmonton upon dry tobacco material shipped from Sweden. As the investigation progressed, however, TTI undertook all the research and development of its pressure vessel (reactor) in Alberta, delivered the equipment to Kentucky, and conducted experimental trials there because, as the Trial Judge accepted as a matter of fact, it was necessary to conduct the experiments in Kentucky to obtain the fresh tobacco needed for the chemical extraction process, with TTI personnel returning to Edmonton on or before December 17 of that year. Ultimately, TTI and the Swedish company ended their relationship, and the reactor was dedicated to the use of a benevolent society for appropriate purposes. For its 1993 taxation year, TTI claimed the amounts associated with the Kentucky operation—which the Federal Court of Appeal ultimately directed be excluded in the sum of $405,967—as qualified SR&ED expenditures eligible for refundable ITCs.

The second cluster of disputed claims involved intercompany management fee charges recorded in both the 1993 and 1994 taxation years. Pursuant to a written Memorandum of Agreement between TTI and its subsidiary TRI, TTI agreed to pay or reimburse 100% of TRI's costs, while simultaneously charging TRI a management fee equal to 30% of all costs incurred by TRI in exchange for research coordination and research management services provided by TTI personnel, principally Mr. DeLong. In its 1993 financial statements, TTI recorded Management Fee Revenue of $199,289.50, which legal counsel later agreed at trial had been mistakenly calculated using a 35% factor rather than the contractual 30% factor, warranting a reduction to $175,628. In its 1994 taxation year, TTI recorded $32,733.94 in management fee revenue charged to TRI. Rather than settling these charges in cash or negotiable instruments, TTI charged the management fees to TRI by accounting entry, and TRI "paid" the fees by bundling them together with its other expenses and charging the entire grossed-up total back to TTI under the cost-reimbursement clause of the Memorandum of Agreement. TTI then claimed the re-charged management fees as qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC purposes in 1993 and 1994.
The Tax Authority's Challenge

The Minister of National Revenue (the "Minister" or the "Crown") reassessed TTI for both the 1993 and 1994 taxation years, disallowing the ITC claims across both expenditure categories. With respect to the 1993 expenditures associated with the Kentucky operation ($405,967), the Minister formally admitted that TTI carried on business in Canada and agreed that the underlying activities satisfied the scientific and technical definition of SR&ED under subsection 37(7) of the Act and section 2900 of the Regulations. However, the Minister challenged the claim on strict territorial grounds. Because those specific experimental activities were physically carried on in Kentucky rather than in Canada, the Minister maintained that the expenditures were made on SR&ED "carried on outside Canada" under subsection 37(2) of the Act rather than on SR&ED "carried on in Canada" under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i). While subsection 37(2) permitted a current deduction in computing business income, expenditures governed by subsection 37(2) could not be taken into account in computing investment tax credits.

With respect to the intercompany management fees ($199,289.50 reduced to $175,628 in 1993, and $32,733.94 in 1994), the Minister challenged the claims on four distinct grounds: first, that the circular accounting entries did not represent genuine expenditures incurred or made by TTI on SR&ED; second, that the management fee charges did not constitute SR&ED or expenditures directly attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED; third, that the amounts were not reasonable in the circumstances; and fourth, for the 1993 taxation year, that even if any portion of the fee were otherwise eligible, it would have to be allocated for ITC purposes in accordance with the proportion of expenditures incurred in Canada versus outside Canada.
Governing Statutory Framework

During the 1993 and 1994 taxation years under review, the statutory architecture governing SR&ED tax incentives operated through the tightly integrated provisions of sections 37, 127, and 248 of the Act and section 2900 of the Regulations. Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) of the Act governed the domestic SR&ED expenditure pool, permitting a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada to deduct expenditures of a current nature made in the year or a preceding taxation year ending after 1973 "on scientific research and experimental development carried on in Canada, directly undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer, and related to a business of the taxpayer". Qualifying expenditures under subsection 37(1) entered the taxpayer's cumulative SR&ED expenditure pool and formed the statutory base for claiming ITCs under section 127, including refundable ITCs available in respect of expenditures on SR&ED carried on in Canada. Conversely, subsection 37(2) of the Act governed foreign research deductions, providing a current-year deduction in computing income for expenditures made on SR&ED "carried on outside Canada," which were excluded from the subsection 37(1) pool and earned no ITCs.

The technical definition of "scientific research and experimental development" was housed in Regulation 2900(1) pursuant to subsection 37(7) (and subsequently subsection 248(1)) of the Act. Regulation 2900(1) defined SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis," encompassing (a) basic research undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view, (b) applied research undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view, and (c) experimental development—"namely, work undertaken for the purposes of achieving technological advancement for the purposes of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products or processes, including incremental improvements thereto"—alongside commensurate support work in paragraph (d). Furthermore, under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) of the Act and subsections 2900(2) and 2900(3) of the Regulations, current expenditures claimed under the traditional method had to be directly attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada—such as hands-on employee remuneration under paragraph 2900(2)(b) or other expenditures directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED under paragraph 2900(2)(c)—or directly attributable to the provision of premises, facilities, or equipment for the prosecution of SR&ED under subsection 2900(3).
Procedural History and Final Judicial Holding

At the Tax Court of Canada in January 1997, Judge Bell delivered a split decision. On the 1993 cross-border expenditures ($405,967), Judge Bell ruled in favour of TTI, holding that the determination of whether an activity constitutes SR&ED under Regulation 2900 must be made by looking at the research project as a whole and not subdividing it into its constituent parts prior to determining whether the expenditure was for work carried on inside or outside Canada. Because TTI's overall project was based in Edmonton, Judge Bell found that the Kentucky experiment was part of the continuous scientific research on tobacco that TTI had commenced in 1990—an isolated and relatively small part of the systematic investigation ongoing in Canada—and allowed the ITCs on those amounts for 1993. Conversely, on the intercompany management fees ($199,289.50 / $175,628 in 1993 and $32,733.94 in 1994), Judge Bell ruled in favour of the Crown, dismissing the 1994 appeal in its entirety and disallowing the 1993 management fees on the ground that the circular accounting entries between TTI and TRI were mere book entries rather than true "expenditures made" on SR&ED.

The Crown appealed Judge Bell's allowance of the 1993 Kentucky expenditures to the Federal Court of Appeal pursuant to section 27 of the Federal Court Act (Dockets A-70-97 and A-303-97), the sole issue on appeal being whether TTI was entitled to ITCs for SR&ED expenditures associated with work done outside Canada. During the period between the January 1997 Tax Court ruling in Tigney and the December 1999 Federal Court of Appeal hearing, a sharp jurisprudential divide emerged in the Tax Court of Canada. In Data Kinetics Ltd. v. The Queen (98 DTC 1877 (TCC)), the Tax Court agreed with Judge Bell's reasoning in Tigney that the research activity should be looked at as a whole and not subdivided into constituent geographic parts. In LGL Limited v. The Queen (Docket 96-4726(IT)G, January 12, 1999), however, the Tax Court declined to follow Tigney and dismissed the taxpayer's claim for ITCs on essential data-collection activities conducted outside Canada.

On February 7, 2000, the Federal Court of Appeal resolved this conflict by dismissing the taxpayer's appeal in LGL Limited and allowing the Crown's appeal in Tigney Technology Incorporated with costs in both the Federal Court of Appeal and the Tax Court of Canada. Writing for a unanimous Court, Justice McDonald expressly rejected the Tax Court reasoning in Tigney and Data Kinetics, holding that the statutory phrase "carried on in Canada" in paragraph 37(1)(a) must be read in its grammatical and ordinary sense in contrast to "carried on outside Canada" in subsection 37(2), requiring that the specific activities giving rise to the claimed expenditure be physically performed within Canada. Consequently, the Tax Court judgment was set aside to the extent of directing that $405,967 be excluded from the qualified expenditures used to calculate TTI's refundable ITCs for its 1993 taxation year; because the sole issue before the Federal Court of Appeal was the treatment of expenditures for work done outside Canada, the appellate ruling did not address the management fee issue decided at trial.

body.text: Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

A rigorous examination of the Tigney Technology litigation demonstrates that the complete disallowance of the taxpayer's ITC claims stemmed not from a failure to demonstrate underlying scientific novelty—indeed, the Crown agreed that the Kentucky technical work in 1993 satisfied the scientific definition of SR&ED—but from profound legal, structural, contractual, and accounting deficiencies.
Territorial Disqualification and the Fallacy of the "Indivisible Project" Theory

The central legal deficiency that defeated TTI's claim at the Federal Court of Appeal was its reliance on a "holistic" or "indivisible project" theory of statutory interpretation to justify executing experimental trials in Kentucky while claiming Canadian ITCs. In constructing its legal position, TTI (alongside the taxpayers in LGL Limited and Data Kinetics Ltd.) advanced a sequential two-step interpretive framework. Under the first step, TTI argued that the determination of whether a project constitutes SR&ED under Regulation 2900(1) must be made prior to any inquiry into whether an expenditure was incurred for work carried on inside or outside Canada. Because Regulation 2900(1) defines SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis," TTI maintained that the project must be taken as an indivisible whole at the initial qualification stage and cannot be subdivided into constituent tasks. Under the second step, TTI contended that once the overarching project is characterized as SR&ED centred in Edmonton, constituent experimental tasks or data collection that had to be performed in Kentucky—and that only became meaningful SR&ED when assimilated into the Canadian project—inherited the Canadian locus of the overall project under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i).

Justice McDonald rejected this interpretive construct by examining the statutory text of section 37 in its entire context. First, the Federal Court of Appeal emphasized that the words "carried on in Canada" in subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) modify "scientific research and experimental development," which refers directly to the physical activities in respect of which the claimed expenditure is incurred. When TTI delivered the pressure vessel it had developed in Alberta to Kentucky and conducted experiments on fresh tobacco in Kentucky, those specific experimental activities were physically carried on outside Canada.

Second, the Court held that treating a multi-jurisdictional project as an indivisible geographical whole would stretch the plain meaning of the Act. Because paragraph 37(1)(a) refers to the total of all amounts each of which is an expenditure, the territorial inquiry focuses on individual expenditures rather than on the project as a whole. A whole-project approach would produce an all-or-nothing result, create uncertainty as to when foreign work is sufficiently integral to a Canadian project, and could equally disallow expenditures clearly connected to SR&ED carried on in Canada, contrary to the Act's purpose of encouraging R&D in Canada. The statutory scheme draws a clear territorial line: subsection 37(1) governs expenditures on SR&ED "carried on in Canada" and confers access to ITCs under section 127, whereas subsection 37(2) governs expenditures on SR&ED "carried on outside Canada" and restricts relief to an income deduction without ITCs. The only criterion is whether the expenditures were made for activities carried on in Canada, even where the foreign work was an essential, non-severable component of a Canadian-directed project that could not be replicated domestically.

Third, the Federal Court of Appeal reconciled the interaction between Regulation 2900 and section 37. Even if an isolated foreign task (such as collecting field data or running a foreign trial) is not standalone SR&ED by itself and only qualifies as SR&ED under Regulation 2900 when assimilated into the overall Canadian project, that assimilation merely establishes that the foreign work is "scientific research and experimental development" rather than routine commercial activity. Once characterized as SR&ED, its physical execution outside Canada places the expenditure squarely within subsection 37(2) ("SR&ED carried on outside Canada") rather than paragraph 37(1)(a) ("SR&ED carried on in Canada"). Because TTI shifted its experimental testing from Edmonton (where initial experiments were performed on dry tobacco shipped from Sweden) to Kentucky, it forfeited ITC eligibility on the $405,967 associated with the Kentucky work, including the direct cost of the data collection and allocable overhead for the work done outside Canada. Moreover, as reflected in Section 6.1 of the Canada Revenue Agency's (CRA) SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy—which explicitly cites Tigney Technology Incorporated v. The Queen, 2000 DTC 6112 (FCA), alongside LGL Ltd. v. The Queen, 2000 DTC 6108 (FCA)—SR&ED overhead and other expenditures related to support work performed outside Canada are deductible only as expenditures on SR&ED carried on outside Canada, are likewise excluded from subsection 37(1), and cannot earn ITCs, even where the cost is incurred or paid in Canada.
Unincurred Intercompany Management Fees and Circular Book-Entry Accounting

The second major pillar of the Tigney Technology litigation—adjudicated by Judge Bell at the Tax Court of Canada and left undisturbed on appeal—exposes a fatal structural flaw in corporate group R&D administration: the reliance on circular, non-arm's length management fees to generate SR&ED expenditure claims. Under the Memorandum of Agreement between TTI and its wholly owned research subsidiary TRI, TRI was established to conduct and account for all research on behalf of TTI, while TTI provided research coordination and management services (performed by Mr. DeLong) to TRI. Rather than paying Mr. DeLong a direct salary from TRI or claiming his direct hands-on salary at TTI, TTI charged TRI a management fee equal to 30% of all of TRI's costs ($199,289.50 booked in 1993 using an erroneous 35% rate and reduced by agreement to $175,628; and $32,733.94 booked in 1994). Simultaneously, the Memorandum of Agreement obligated TTI to pay 100% of TRI's costs.

As established during cross-examination at trial, if TRI incurred $100,000 of direct research expenditures, TTI would charge TRI a $30,000 management fee by accounting entry, and TRI would "pay" that fee simply by charging the $30,000 management fee together with the $100,000 of other expenses right back to TTI. Judge Bell held that these circular transactions were mere book entries rather than genuine "expenditures made" or incurred on SR&ED under paragraph 37(1)(a). Relying on the legal principles applied in Ed Sinclair Construction & Supplies Ltd. et al., Judge Bell noted that while a payment or receipt can occur without physical currency where there is a transfer of a negotiable instrument or a bona fide settlement of commercial obligations that represents and produces money and is treated as such by business persons, a self-cancelling accounting loop between a parent and subsidiary creates no economic outlay.

Beyond the absence of a bona fide outlay, TTI's management fee structure violated the substantive expenditure rules under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) of the Act and subsections 2900(2)(b) and 2900(2)(c) of the Regulations. Under the traditional method, an expenditure must satisfy two strict tests to be considered "directly attributable" to the prosecution of SR&ED: first, it must be directly related to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (connecting directly to the SR&ED work, the SR&ED staff, or the machinery/equipment used for SR&ED, with no intervening step or intermediary); and second, it must be incremental, meaning the expenditure would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED not occurred. Applying an arbitrary flat 30% or 35% percentage surcharge across all of a subsidiary's costs fails to establish a reasonable, non-arbitrary direct linkage to hands-on SR&ED prosecution. Furthermore, TTI's witness admitted that the management fee was used in lieu of salary as a mechanism to obtain money for research coordination and management services, thereby conflating direct hands-on technical supervision with general corporate administration, budgeting, and cost control—activities that have only an indirect link to SR&ED and are disallowed. Compounding these substantive defects were severe evidentiary and procedural lapses: TTI's accountants erroneously applied a 35% markup in 1993 instead of the contractual 30% rate, failed to segregate management charges attributable to Kentucky testing versus Canadian testing, and filed inaccurate pleadings that forced the Tax Court to expend considerable time reconciling the issues at trial.
Evolution of Statutory Safe Harbours and Anti-Markup Rules Following Tigney Technology

The strict holdings in Tigney Technology and LGL Limited generated significant second- and third-order consequences for Canadian tax policy and audit administration. Recognizing that the absolute territorial bar of Tigney Technology penalized Canadian businesses when Canadian-resident employees had to travel briefly outside Canada to perform integral testing, Parliament subsequently enacted subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) of the Act, which deem salary or wages paid after February 25, 2008 to Canadian-resident employees for SR&ED carried on outside Canada that directly supports the taxpayer's SR&ED carried on in Canada to be expenditures on SR&ED carried on in Canada, but strictly limit the eligible foreign salary to 10% of the claimant's total domestic SR&ED salaries and wages. Outside that narrow 10% domestic-resident wage window, however, Tigney Technology remains the governing law in Canada: all foreign subcontractor fees, foreign facility charges, foreign materials, foreign travel and lodging expenses, and employee wages exceeding the 10% cap remain relegated to subsection 37(2) and are barred from earning ITCs. Similarly, in the context of non-arm's length intercompany R&D contracts, modern statutory rules under subsections 127(9) and 127(11.6) reinforce Judge Bell's disallowance of TTI's management fee by stripping out any intercompany markup between non-arm's length corporations and requiring formal expenditure transfer agreements under subsection 127(13).
Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory requirement examined in Tigney Technology Incorporated (across both the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal) against the taxpayer's specific legal or evidentiary deficiency and the governing judicial standard of proof established by the courts.

headers: Taxpayer's Specific Failure in Tigney Technology Inc.
Judicial Standard of Proof & Governing Legal Rule

cells: Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) vs. Subsection 37(2) of the Income Tax Act: Territorial requirement that SR&ED be physically "carried on in Canada" to qualify for Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) under s. 127.

TTI conducted initial experiments on dry tobacco in Edmonton but delivered its Alberta-developed pressure vessel to Kentucky and conducted experiments there on fresh tobacco ($405,967 in 1993). TTI argued the project was an indivisible whole centred in Canada.

Activity-by-Activity Physical Locus Test: The words "carried on in Canada" must be read in their ordinary grammatical sense in contrast to "carried on outside Canada" in s. 37(2). A project must be subdivided into constituent geographical activities; work physically performed abroad falls under s. 37(2) (no ITCs), even if essential to a Canadian project.
Subsection 37(7) / 248(1) of the Act & Section 2900(1) of the Income Tax Regulations: Definition of SR&ED and sequencing of project qualification vs. territoriality.

TTI asserted that Regulation 2900(1) applies first to qualify an entire project as an undivided whole, and that once qualified as a Canadian project, constituent foreign tasks automatically inherit Canadian status.

Project-Level Qualification, Expenditure-Level Territoriality: Regulation 2900 requires cogent evidence of systematic investigation. The Regulation 2900 determination is made on the project as a whole and is irrelevant to where the work is done; dividing costs between work in and outside Canada does not affect the project's SR&ED status. While overall project context in Canada may establish that a foreign task supports SR&ED, Regulation 2900 cannot override the geographic exclusion in s. 37(1)(a).
Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) of the Act ("Expenditure ... Made"): Requirement that a claimed amount be a genuine economic expenditure incurred and paid by the taxpayer.

TTI charged its subsidiary TRI a management fee ($199,289.50 / $175,628 in 1993; $32,733.94 in 1994) via journal entry, and TRI "paid" it solely by charging 100% of its costs (including the fee) back to TTI.

Bona Fide Economic Outlay Standard: Relying on Ed Sinclair Construction, circular book entries that self-cancel between a parent and subsidiary without transferring money, negotiable instruments, or genuine economic value are mere book entries, not "expenditures made" on SR&ED.

Subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) of the Act & Subsections 2900(2)(b)–(c) of the Regulations: Requirement that salaries and overhead be "directly attributable" (directly related and incremental) to the prosecution of SR&ED.

Instead of paying direct salary to Mr. DeLong and tracking hands-on SR&ED supervision hours, TTI levied an arbitrary flat percentage markup (30% contractual; 35% actually booked in 1993) across all of TRI's costs.

Direct Linkage & Incremental Cost Standard: Remuneration must reflect actual hands-on undertaking, supervision, or support of SR&ED. Other expenditures under Reg. 2900(2)(c) require proof of direct linkage (no intermediary step) and incrementality (would not have been incurred but for SR&ED). Arbitrary percentage markups are disallowed.
Section 67 of the Act & Regulation 2900(2): Reasonableness of expenditures and accuracy of intercompany cost allocations between domestic and foreign activities.

TTI mistakenly applied a 35% markup in 1993 ($199,289.50) instead of the 30% rate in the Memorandum of Agreement ($175,628), failed to segregate domestic vs. foreign management effort, and presented defective pleadings at trial.

Substantiated Allocation & Contractual Precision: The claimant bears the burden of explaining how allocations are determined and providing contemporaneous job-costing support. Overhead or management costs tied to foreign non-qualifying work under s. 37(2) must be carved out of the s. 37(1) ITC base.

body.text: Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To illustrate how Canadian taxpayers and their tax advisors can proactively structure R&D operations to overcome the legal and evidentiary pitfalls identified in Tigney Technology Incorporated, the following two industry case studies replicate the exact vulnerabilities of the ruling—first, cross-border experimental execution in a bioprocess engineering project, and second, circular intercompany management fees in a multi-entity technology group—and demonstrate step-by-step how to achieve full statutory compliance under the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations.
Case Study 1: Bioprocess & Clean-Tech Chemical Extraction (Overcoming Territorial Disqualification under Subsections 37(1), 37(1.4), 37(1.5), and 37(2))
Baseline Scenario and Identified Tigney Vulnerability

PrairieFraction BioSolutions Inc. ("PFB") is a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) headquartered in Edmonton, Alberta. PFB is developing a proprietary supercritical carbon dioxide and subcritical water hydrolysis process to fractionate agricultural biomass and isolate bioactive polyphenols without thermal degradation of heat-sensitive oligomers. A European nutraceutical manufacturer based in Uppsala, Sweden ("NordicNutra AB") contacts PFB to investigate whether PFB's reactor technology can extract an unstable glycoside from freshly pressed Nordic bilberry pomace. Because fresh bilberry pomace undergoes rapid enzymatic oxidation within hours of pressing, PFB's engineering team proposes to ship a pilot extraction reactor to NordicNutra's facility in Sweden, lease laboratory space and local technicians in Uppsala for four months, and send two Edmonton chemical engineers to Sweden to execute the experimental campaign at a total cost of $450,000. PFB's management assumes that because the core extraction technology was conceived in Edmonton and the resulting data will be analyzed in Canada, the entire $450,000 campaign qualifies as part of an indivisible Canadian SR&ED project under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i).

Under the Federal Court of Appeal's holding in Tigney Technology Inc. and LGL Limited, this operational plan is fatally flawed. The CRA will subdivide the project into its geographic components and reclassify all expenditures incurred for experimental activities physically performed in Sweden—including foreign facility charges, Swedish technician fees, consumables used in Sweden, travel and lodging, and employee wages exceeding the 10% statutory cap—into subsection 37(2) as SR&ED carried on outside Canada, completely eliminating PFB's ITC entitlement on the Swedish campaign.
Step 1: Project Governance and Experimental Location Re-Engineering

To satisfy the strict physical locus requirement of subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) ("carried on in Canada"), PFB must restructure its project governance so that the systematic investigation by means of experiment or analysis takes place physically inside its Edmonton facility rather than in Sweden. Just as TTI's initial experiments in Edmonton on dry tobacco shipped from Sweden were undisputedly "carried on in Canada" prior to TTI moving its reactor trials to Kentucky, PFB must bring the foreign raw material to Canada rather than moving its reactor and personnel to Europe. PFB's chemical engineers establish a cryogenic flash-freezing and inert-nitrogen packaging protocol that arrests enzymatic oxidation in freshly pressed bilberry pomace immediately at the Swedish press line. NordicNutra flash-freezes and air-freights 2,000 kilograms of stabilized bilberry pomace in liquid-nitrogen dry shippers to PFB's laboratory in Edmonton. At the Edmonton pilot plant, PFB engineers thaw the feedstock under controlled inert-gas conditions to replicate the exact biochemical boundary conditions of fresh pomace and conduct all supercritical extraction runs domestically. By domesticating the physical execution of the experiments, 100% of the Edmonton laboratory wages, utilities, and the cost of the imported bilberry pomace consumed or transformed in the Edmonton reactor qualify as SR&ED carried on in Canada under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) and subsection 2900(2) of the Regulations.
Step 2: Strategic Governance of Unavoidable Foreign Tasks Under Subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5)

Where a brief 10-day on-site verification at NordicNutra's press line in Uppsala remains scientifically indispensable to calibrate inline moisture and enzymatic sensors prior to flash-freezing, PFB must govern the foreign trip strictly within the statutory parameters of subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) of the Act and Section 6.3 of the CRA's SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy. PFB restricts the Uppsala sensor-calibration trip exclusively to T4 salaried employees who are residents of Canada (its two Edmonton chemical engineers) and engages zero Swedish subcontractors or foreign personnel, because third-party foreign payments are entirely excluded from subsection 37(1.5). Furthermore, PFB monitors its domestic SR&ED salary base to ensure strict adherence to the 10% wage ceiling. Given $800,000 of eligible T4 salaries for hands-on SR&ED physically performed in Edmonton during the fiscal year, PFB's maximum permissible foreign SR&ED wage claim under subsection 37(1.5) is $80,000. Because the 10-day Swedish calibration trip represents only $12,000 of direct engineering wages, the entire $12,000 is statutorily deemed to be SR&ED carried on in Canada and qualifies for ITCs. In accordance with Section 6.3 of the CRA's SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy, PFB excludes foreign airfare, hotel lodging, meals, and any foreign non-SR&ED overhead from its traditional overhead claim, or elects the Prescribed Proxy Method under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) so that notional overhead is computed cleanly as a percentage of eligible salaries.
Step 3: Contractual Restructuring to Preserve IP Entitlement and Avoid Funded Research Reductions

Although the Federal Court of Appeal in Tigney Technology decided only whether expenditures associated with work done outside Canada qualified for ITCs, the taxpayer's collaboration with Swedish Tobacco illustrates the importance of commercial exploitation rights and expenditure nexus. Under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) of the Act, the SR&ED must be related to a business of the claimant, and under subsection 127(9) of the Act, any contract payment or reimbursement received for performing SR&ED grinds down the qualified expenditure pool. PFB therefore avoids entering into a fee-for-service testing contract with NordicNutra AB. Instead, PFB and NordicNutra execute a Joint Collaboration and Licensing Option Agreement under which PFB bears 100% of the financial cost of the Edmonton extraction trials, retains sole legal and beneficial ownership of all background and foreground intellectual property developed in Edmonton, and grants NordicNutra an option to negotiate a commercial royalty-bearing license if the technological uncertainties are resolved.
Step 4: Contemporaneous Documentation and Activity-Level Experimentation Tracking

To meet the evidentiary threshold of Regulation 2900—which, as noted in Tigney Technology, requires the taxpayer to adduce cogent evidence of systematic investigation—PFB implements rigorous activity-level documentation that proves both technological advancement and geographic locus. Every experimental run conducted in Edmonton is logged contemporaneously in an Electronic Laboratory Notebook capturing the specific technological uncertainty (oligomer thermal degradation thresholds), the formulated hypothesis, the exact reactor pressures and co-solvent ratios tested, and the resulting HPLC chromatograms. Concurrently, PFB's payroll and project-costing system segregates employee time daily across three separate ledger codes: domestic hands-on experimentation in Edmonton (SR-CAN-37(1)), permissible Canadian-resident employee calibration work in Sweden within the 10% cap (SR-FOR-37(1.4)), and excluded foreign travel or non-qualifying support (EXCL-37(2)), ensuring an unassailable audit trail.
Case Study 2: Multi-Entity Enterprise Hardware & Firmware R&D Group (Eliminating Circular Intercompany Management Fees & Qualifying Non-Arm's Length SR&ED)
Baseline Scenario and Identified Tigney Vulnerability

Apex Grid Technologies Inc. ("Apex Parent") is a Canadian corporation based in Kanata, Ontario, engaged in developing solid-state fault-current limiters for high-voltage microgrids. Apex Parent owns 100% of the shares of Apex LabWorks Inc. ("Apex Sub"), a subsidiary established to conduct and account for all laboratory prototyping on behalf of Apex Parent. While 18 junior electrical engineers are employed on the payroll of Apex Sub (incurring $1,500,000 in direct wages and prototype materials), the three senior technical directors—Dr. Vance (Chief Scientist), Ms. Chen (VP of Power Electronics), and Mr. Patel (Lead Firmware Architect)—remain on the payroll of Apex Parent alongside corporate administrative personnel. Under an intercompany Memorandum of Agreement modelled directly on the arrangement in Tigney Technology, Apex Parent agrees to pay 100% of Apex Sub's costs while charging Apex Sub a flat 30% management fee ($450,000) for research coordination and management services. At year-end, Apex Parent records $450,000 of management fee revenue via a journal entry debiting Apex Sub, and Apex Sub "pays" the fee by bundling the $450,000 with its $1,500,000 of direct lab expenses and charging the entire $1,950,000 back to Apex Parent via an intercompany loan account offset. Apex Parent then claims the full $1,950,000 for SR&ED ITCs.

Under Judge Bell's ruling in Tigney Technology Inc. (which was not before the Federal Court of Appeal, whose sole issue was ITC entitlement for work done outside Canada), the $450,000 management fee will be disallowed in full. First, because the $450,000 charge was merely recorded via circular book entries between Apex Parent and Apex Sub without any transfer of money or negotiable instruments, it is not an "expenditure made" on SR&ED under paragraph 37(1)(a) and the rule in Ed Sinclair Construction. Second, levying an arbitrary 30% percentage surcharge across all subsidiary costs fails the "directly related" and "incremental" requirements of Regulation 2900(2)(c) and improperly bundles non-qualifying corporate administration with technical supervision. Third, under the non-arm's length contract rules in subsections 127(9) and 127(11.6) of the Act, any intercompany markup charged between related corporations is statutorily excluded from qualified expenditures.
Step 1: Dismantling the Circular Management Fee and Aligning Direct T4 Payroll with Technical Execution

To cure the foundational defect identified in Tigney Technology—where the taxpayer charged an intercompany management fee instead of paying direct salary for research supervision—Apex Group immediately amends its intercompany Memorandum of Agreement to repeal the 30% management fee clause. In its place, Apex Group aligns T4 employment compensation directly with the entity claiming the hands-on technical work under Regulation 2900(2)(b). Either Dr. Vance, Ms. Chen, and Mr. Patel are placed directly onto the T4 payroll of Apex Sub (so that Apex Sub directly incurs and pays their salaries alongside the 18 junior engineers), or they remain on the T4 payroll of Apex Parent and Apex Parent claims their actual, substantiated hands-on SR&ED supervision salaries directly on Apex Parent's own Form T661 under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) as SR&ED directly undertaken by Apex Parent.
Step 2: Restructuring Intercompany Funding via Cash-Settled Subcontracts and Subsection 127(13) Transfer Agreements

Where commercial and intellectual-property governance requires Apex Parent to hold all patents and claim the consolidated ITCs for the corporate group, the financial flow between Apex Parent and Apex Sub must satisfy both the common-law outlay standard applied in Tigney Technology and the statutory non-arm's length SR&ED rules. Apex Parent and Apex Sub execute a written Intercompany R&D Performance Agreement specifying that Apex Sub performs SR&ED in Canada on behalf of Apex Parent at actual cost ($1,500,000), with zero intercompany management fee loop. Each month, Apex Sub issues an itemized invoice supported by payroll registers and vendor receipts, and Apex Parent settles the exact invoice amount via an actual bank wire transfer from Apex Parent's operating bank account to Apex Sub's operating bank account prior to fiscal year-end, satisfying the Ed Sinclair Construction and Tigney Technology requirement for a genuine economic outlay. Because payments between non-arm's length corporations are excluded from the statutory definition of "contract payment" under subsection 127(9), Apex Sub and Apex Parent jointly execute and file Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) pursuant to subsection 127(13) of the Act, legally transferring the $1,500,000 of qualified expenditures incurred by Apex Sub to Apex Parent for ITC computation, while Apex Parent directly claims the $360,000 of eligible hands-on T4 salaries of Dr. Vance, Ms. Chen, and Mr. Patel on its own T661 return.
Step 3: Segregating Hands-On Technical Supervision from Non-Qualifying Corporate Administration

To ensure that the $360,000 of senior architect compensation at Apex Parent satisfies subsections 2900(2)(b) and 2900(2)(c) of the Regulations and survives audit scrutiny under the CRA's SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy, Apex Parent enforces a strict functional separation between direct technical supervision and corporate management. Only the hours devoted by Dr. Vance, Ms. Chen, and Mr. Patel to directly undertaking, supervising, or supporting the hands-on prosecution of SR&ED—such as mathematically modelling fault-current interruption transients, analyzing failed semiconductor die assemblies, and directing firmware algorithm iterations—are claimed as direct SR&ED salary. Conversely, all time spent by the three executives on non-technological feasibility studies, bidding, initiation and closing of licensing agreements, commercialization of existing intellectual property, review and approval of SR&ED budgets, cost control, and patent applications is excluded from the claim, as these activities have only an indirect link to SR&ED and are explicitly disallowed. To avoid disputes over whether clerical or administrative support costs meet the strict two-prong "directly related" and "incremental" tests of Regulation 2900(2)(c) under the traditional method, both Apex Parent and Apex Sub elect the Prescribed Proxy Method under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B), calculating eligible overhead strictly by reference to their substantiated hands-on T4 SR&ED salary base.
Step 4: Implementing Granular Time-Tracking and Pre-Filing Accounting Reconciliation Controls

In Tigney Technology, the taxpayer's credibility at trial was severely damaged by accounting errors—specifically applying a 35% markup rate instead of the contractual 30% rate—and by pleadings that failed to reconcile the disputed figures prior to the hearing. To eliminate such evidentiary failures, Apex Group deploys an integrated time-tracking and job-costing protocol across both corporations. Dr. Vance, Ms. Chen, and Mr. Patel log their hours weekly against specific experimental work packages in the engineering repository, providing contemporaneous proof of the exact proportion of their time devoted to hands-on SR&ED prosecution versus excluded corporate management (analogous to the 60% hands-on allocation methodology validated in the CRA's SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy). Prior to filing the corporate tax returns, external tax counsel performs a comprehensive pre-filing audit reconciling the general ledger accounts, intercompany bank wire confirmations, T4 payroll summaries, and Form T1146 transfer schedules dollar-for-dollar, ensuring complete mathematical and legal precision.

cells: Cross-Border Experimental Execution
Moving experimental reactor runs and personnel to Kentucky; claiming foreign tasks as part of an "indivisible" Canadian project under s. 37(1)(a).
Importing stabilized raw feedstock/samples to Canada for domestic testing under s. 37(1)(a); restricting unavoidable foreign trips to Canadian-resident T4 employees within the 10% cap of s. 37(1.5).
Executive Technical Supervision Remuneration
Charging an arbitrary 30% (or erroneous 35%) intercompany management fee across all subsidiary costs in lieu of paying direct T4 salary.
Paying direct T4 salary from the claiming/performing entity and claiming only contemporaneously tracked hours of hands-on technical direction under Reg. 2900(2)(b).
Intercompany Cost Settlement Mechanism
Circular journal entries where Parent charges Subsidiary a fee and Subsidiary "pays" by re-billing 100% of its grossed-up costs back to Parent.
Eliminating circular markups; settling actual cost-reimbursement invoices via real cash wire transfers supported by a formal s. 127(13) Transfer Agreement (Form T1146).
Overhead & Indirect Cost Allocation
Bundling general corporate administration and foreign project management into an unallocated percentage markup.
Electing the Prescribed Proxy Method or proving strict direct linkage and incrementality under Reg. 2900(2)(c) while carving out all s. 37(2) foreign overhead.

body.text: Conclusion

The judicial history of Tigney Technology Incorporated—encompassing both the January 1997 Tax Court of Canada judgment and the February 2000 Federal Court of Appeal reversal—establishes an essential operational mandate for Canadian corporations and their tax advisors. Crucially, the ruling demonstrates that satisfying the scientific and technological criteria of Regulation 2900(1) is a necessary but insufficient condition for securing Canadian SR&ED Investment Tax Credits. Even where the Crown formally agrees that the taxpayer's experimental work constitutes genuine SR&ED, the claim will be completely disqualified if the experimental activities are physically executed outside Canada in violation of subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) or if the claimed costs are generated through circular intercompany bookkeeping rather than bona fide economic outlays.

To safeguard SR&ED claims against the legal pitfalls established in Tigney Technology, Canadian claimants must integrate three structural controls into their R&D governance. First, because Canadian courts reject the "indivisible project" theory and apply the "carried on in Canada" test on an activity-by-activity basis, taxpayers must engineer their experimental protocols to import foreign test materials and replicate boundary conditions inside Canadian laboratories whenever feasible, confining any unavoidable foreign tasks strictly to Canadian-resident T4 employees within the 10% wage limit of subsection 37(1.5). Second, corporate groups must eliminate percentage-based intercompany management fees and circular journal-entry offsets between parent and subsidiary entities, compensating senior technical leaders through direct T4 salary supported by contemporaneous time records that segregate hands-on technical supervision from excluded corporate administration. Finally, where multi-entity or cross-border operations are unavoidable, claimants must settle intercompany R&D obligations in cash, execute formal expenditure transfer agreements under subsection 127(13), and maintain granular job-costing ledgers that cleanly isolate subsection 37(1) domestic expenditures and overhead from subsection 37(2) foreign deductions prior to filing.
